A deity is a god or goddess — a supernatural, divine being that is believed to have powers far beyond those of any human or natural creature, and that is typically worshipped by people as a higher power.

Think of it this way: a deity is not just a powerful character from a story. A deity is a being that people genuinely believe in, pray to, offer respect to, and consider to be sacred.

For a being to be called a deity, people generally associate it with some or all of these qualities:

Supernatural power. A deity can do things that no human, animal, or natural force can do on its own — controlling the weather, creating life, deciding fate, and so on.

Immortality. Deities do not die the way humans do. They are either eternal (they have always existed and always will) or at least ageless and undying by nature.

Dominion over something. Many deities are believed to rule over a specific domain — love, war, the sea, the sun, death, wisdom, fertility, and so on. For example, in ancient Greek belief, Poseidon was the deity of the sea.

Worship. Humans recognise a deity as worthy of reverence, prayer, rituals, or offerings. This relationship between humans and a deity — where humans look up to, fear, love, or depend on the deity — is a key part of what defines one.

A nature above the human. A deity exists on a completely different level from humans. It is not simply a very strong or very wise person — it belongs to a different category of existence altogether.
The Two Main Ways "Deity" Is Used

1. To refer to a specific divine being

Here, "deity" simply means one particular god or goddess.

  • "Apollo was a deity worshipped in ancient Greece."
  • "Many cultures have a deity associated with the harvest season."
  • "She prayed to the deity of her ancestors."

In this sense, "a deity" works exactly like saying "a god" or "a goddess." You can swap them in most sentences and mean the same thing.

2. To refer to the concept or nature of being divine

Here, "deity" is used more abstractly — not to point to a specific being, but to talk about divinity itself, or the supreme divine force.

  • "He spent his life questioning the existence of deity."
  • "The concept of deity is central to most religions."

In this use, it is similar to saying "godhood" or "the divine." It refers to the quality or state of being a god, rather than naming a particular one.

"A deity" (with the indefinite article a) refers to one god or goddess among many — or just a single divine being in general. This is common when talking about polytheistic religions (religions with many gods).

  • "Mars was a deity of war in Roman religion."

"The Deity" (often with a capital D and the definite article the) is used in monotheistic contexts (religions with one God) to refer to the one supreme divine being — basically, another way of saying "God."

  • "The Deity is believed to be all-knowing and all-powerful."

These words are closely related, but not identical:

God / Goddess — These are the everyday, familiar words for a divine being. "Deity" is the more formal, scholarly, or neutral version. When a historian, philosopher, or academic is discussing religion without favouring any particular faith, they often use "deity" because it feels more objective and universal.

Divine being — This is a descriptive phrase that means the same thing. "Deity" is simply the single-word version of it.

Spirit / Ghost — These are supernatural, but they are not deities. A spirit may linger after death; a ghost may haunt a place. But they are not worshipped as gods and do not hold power over the universe or nature.

Demigod — A being that is partly divine (often the child of a deity and a human). A demigod has some divine qualities but is not a full deity.

Idol — An idol is a physical object or image that represents a deity. The idol itself is not the deity.
How Deities Appear Across Different Beliefs

Polytheism (belief in many gods): In ancient Greece, Rome, Egypt, India, Norse culture, and many others, there were entire families or networks of deities — each governing a different part of the world or human life. Zeus, Odin, Ra, Vishnu, and Ares are all deities.

Monotheism (belief in one God): In religions like Christianity, Islam, and Judaism, there is only one deity — referred to as God. The word "deity" is still used in scholarly discussions to refer to this one supreme being.

Hinduism: A nuanced example — there is one ultimate supreme reality (Brahman), but it is expressed and worshipped through many deities (Shiva, Vishnu, Lakshmi, Durga, and hundreds more).

Atheism: The belief that no deities exist at all.

Agnosticism: The position that the existence of a deity is unknown or unknowable.

• One divine being → a deity
  • More than one → deities

Example: "The ancient Romans worshipped dozens of deities."

• "In many ancient cultures, the sun was seen as a deity that gave life to the earth."
  • "Different religions have very different ideas about what a deity is and how one should be worshipped."
  • "Some philosophers argue that the existence of a deity cannot be proven or disproven."
  • "She studied the deities of the Aztec civilisation for her history class."
  • "The temple was built to honour the local deity."
  • "He did not believe in any deity, but he respected those who did."
  • "Artists throughout history have tried to capture the image of deity in sculpture and painting."

If you had to reduce it to its absolute essence:

A deity is a divine, supernatural being — a god or goddess — that is believed to hold great power over the world or some part of it, and that people worship or revere as sacred.

Everything else above is just the full picture of what that really means in practice.
